title: Nanobiomechanics in Oncology: Atomic Force Microscopy for Cancer Mechanophenotyping Using Cellular Young's Modulus

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Nanobiomechanics in Oncology: Atomic Force Microscopy for Cancer Mechanophenotyping Using Cellular Young's Modulus》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · snz270090-sec-0001-p1】Cancer remains a major global health burden, accounting for approximately one in six deaths worldwide (World Health Organization 2026). Prognosis is strongly influenced by the stage at diagnosis, with metastatic disease being responsible for most cancer‐related mortality (Eccles and Welch 2007; World Health Organization 2026). Earlier identification of malignant transformation is therefore critical to improving treatment outcomes. Histopathological examination of tissue remains the gold standard for cancer diagnosis and grading and provides important prognostic information (He et al. 2012), often supplemented by techniques such as immunohistochemistry (Oliveira and Ribeiro‐Silva 2011; Selves et al. 2018). However, these approaches generally require tissue biopsy and primarily assess morphological and molecular abnormalities that are already detectable within the sampled tissue. There is consequently considerable interest in identifying complementary biomarkers capable of detecting earlier cellular changes associated with carcinogenesis.

【Cell Biomechanics and Cancer · snz270090-sec-0002-p2】These structural alterations are reflected in measurable changes in cellular mechanical properties, including elasticity, viscoelasticity, adhesion and deformability (Suresh 2007). Among these, cellular stiffness or elasticity has been particularly widely investigated (Zhou et al. 2025). Young's modulus is commonly used as an apparent measure of cellular stiffness, relating applied mechanical loading to the resulting deformation within an assumed elastic model. However, living cells are intrinsically viscoelastic, heterogeneous and dynamically remodelling materials rather than ideal elastic solids (Eliahoo et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2025). Consequently, Young's modulus obtained from cellular measurements is dependent on the measurement technique, probing scale, loading rate, indentation depth and modelling assumptions and is most appropriately interpreted as an apparent mechanical parameter for comparisons made under defined experimental conditions.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Nanobiomechanics in Oncology: Atomic Force Microscopy for Cancer Mechanophenotyping Using Cellular Young's Modulus》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Literature Search and Selection Methods · snz270090-sec-0004-p1】The aim of this narrative review was to critically evaluate the literature on the use of AFM to characterise Young's modulus in cancer‐related cellular and tissue models, with particular emphasis on its potential diagnostic and translational significance. A structured electronic literature search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar to identify relevant studies published between 1999 and 2025. Searches used combinations of controlled vocabulary, where applicable and free‐text terms including ‘AFM', ‘neoplasm', ‘cancer', ‘elastic modulus', Young's modulus' and cell biomechanics;. Reference lists of relevant primary studies and review articles were also manually screened to identify additional eligible publications.

【Literature Search and Selection Methods · snz270090-sec-0004-p2】Studies were included if they reported AFM‐based measurements of Young's modulus in human cancer‐related models and compared mechanical properties between non‐malignant and malignant cells or tissues, or across different pathological stages, histological grades or metastatic phenotypes. Review articles, non‐human studies, non‐English‐language publications and studies that did not report AFM‐derived Young's modulus were excluded from the primary study synthesis. Review articles were nevertheless used to provide background context and to identify additional primary studies. Figure 3 summarises the literature search and study‐selection process.

【Results · snz270090-sec-0005-p1】Table 1 summarises the included AFM studies reporting Young's modulus in cancer‐related models.

【Conclusion · snz270090-sec-0014-p1】AFM studies across diverse cancer models demonstrate that malignant transformation is frequently accompanied by substantial alterations in cellular mechanics, with reduced Young's modulus representing a common but not universal phenotype. The accumulated evidence indicates that cancer mechanics are better understood as a dynamic and heterogeneous mechanophenotype rather than as a simple transition from stiff normal cells to soft malignant cells. Disease stage, cytoskeletal organisation, cellular region, microenvironment and measurement methodology all influence the apparent mechanical state. The potential diagnostic value of Young's modulus is therefore unlikely to reside in a universal cut‐off. Instead, stiffness should be integrated with complementary parameters, including spatial mechanical heterogeneity, viscoelasticity, adhesion, deformation energy and nanotopography. Advances in automation, high‐throughput force acquisition and artificial intelligence are progressively mitigating some of the traditional limitations of cellular AFM and may enable mechanical characterisation across substantially larger cell populations. The next phase of the field should therefore move beyond demonstrating mechanical differences between normal and cancer cells towards establishing standardised, reproducible and clinically validated multidimensional mechanophenotypes in patient‐derived specimens.

AFM studies across diverse cancer models demonstrate that malignant transformation is frequently accompanied by substantial alterations in cellular mechanics, with reduced Young's modulus representing a common but not universal phenotype. The accumulated evidence indicates that cancer mechanics are better understood as a dynamic and heterogeneous mechanophenotype rather than as a simple transition from stiff normal cells to soft malignant cells. Disease stage, cytoskeletal organisation, cellular region, microenvironment and measurement methodology all influence the apparent mechanical state. The potential diagnostic value of Young's modulus is therefore unlikely to reside in a universal cut‐off. Instead, stiffness should be integrated with complementary parameters, including spatial mechanical heterogeneity, viscoelasticity, adhesion, deformation energy and nanotopography. Advances in automation, high‐throughput force acquisition and artificial intelligence are progressively mitigating some of the traditional limitations of cellular AFM and may enable mechanical characterisation across substantially larger cell populations. The next phase of the field should therefore move beyond demonstrating mechanical differences between normal and cancer cells towards establishing standardised, reproducible and clinically validated multidimensional mechanophenotypes in patient‐derived specimens.

【FIGURE 1 · snz270090-fig-0001】FIGURE 1 Schematic illustration of AFM. (1) and (2) Interaction of the AFM tip with the sample/cell causes cantilever deflection, which is detected as a change in the laser signal at the photodiode (created with BioRender.com). (3) and (4) 2D and 3D representations for cells.

【FIGURE 2 · snz270090-fig-0002】FIGURE 2 Schematic AFM force–distance curve. The curve represents the interaction between the AFM tip and the sample surface during approach and retraction. On the x‐axis is the tip–sample separation distance, and on the y‐axis is the force applied to the cantilever. During the approach, the tip initially experiences no force, followed by a small attractive regime (negative force) as van der Waals and other interactions pull the tip towards the surface. Upon contact, the tip exerts a repulsive force on the sample, with the slope indicating sample stiffness. During retraction, adhesive interactions can temporarily pull the tip towards the surface, producing an adhesion peak (maximum negative force) before the force returns to zero. Key features, including the contact point, repulsive regime, attractive regime and adhesion force, are labelled, illustrating how AFM force–distance curves can be used to measure mechanical properties such as cellular stiffness (Young's modulus) and surface adhesion.

【FIGURE 3 · snz270090-fig-0003】FIGURE 3 Literature search and study‐selection flow diagram.
